opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think data efficiency is one of the most underrated directions right now. For a long time the default recipe was to scale everything: more parameters, more compute, more tokens. That worked remarkably well, and I don't think anyone should dismiss it. But at some point you run into the reality that high-quality data is finite. You can't keep assuming there's another ten trillion good tokens lying around.

So the question becomes: how do you get more out of every token you train on? There are a few angles I find interesting. One is the objective itself. Back when we worked on things like UL2, a big part of the motivation was that the standard next-token objective isn't necessarily the most sample-efficient way to learn. Mixing denoising objectives, different corruption spans, different "modes," can give the model richer learning signals from the same data. I still think there's a lot of headroom in objective design that people kind of stopped exploring because causal LM just worked and was simple.

The second angle is data quality and curation. People sometimes treat data as this boring plumbing problem, but honestly it's where a lot of the real gains are. Filtering, deduplication, mixture ratios, figuring out which domains actually move capabilities. Many times you get a bigger jump from fixing the data mixture than from some clever architecture tweak.

Third is multi-epoch training and synthetic data. The old intuition was "never repeat data," but it's more nuanced than that. Repeating good data a few times is often fine, and synthetic data, when it's done carefully, can help, though you have to be careful about collapse and about the model just learning its own quirks.

And then architecturally, I'm always a bit skeptical of claims that some new architecture is dramatically more data efficient, because a lot of those results don't hold up at scale. The real test is whether it still wins when you've tuned the baseline properly and trained at meaningful compute. So my general view is: be empirical, be honest with baselines, and focus on the things that compound, which are usually objectives and data, not flashy tricks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving data efficiency through objectives, curation, repeated or synthetic data, and empirical evaluation; it does not frame the task as identifying a concrete bug to fix.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think data efficiency is one of those things that everyone agrees is important but it's actually kind of underrated in terms of how much leverage it gives you. The way I think about it is, we've spent a long time in a regime where the answer to almost everything was just "more tokens." Scale the data, scale the compute, and the loss goes down. And that works, right? Scaling laws are real. But the thing people sometimes forget is that the high-quality data on the internet is actually finite. You can keep scraping, but at some point you're just adding noise, and you start seeing diminishing returns per token much faster than you'd expect.

So for me, data efficiency really splits into a few things. One is the obvious one, which is just quality. How much signal are you getting per token? And honestly, a lot of the gains that people attribute to architecture or to clever training tricks, when you dig into it, it's really the data mixture that moved the needle. I've seen this over and over, both at Google and at Reka. You change the mixture, you filter more aggressively, and suddenly a model that's a fraction of the size is matching something much bigger. That's the stuff that doesn't show up in papers as much because it's kind of boring and very empirical, but it's where a lot of the real work is.

The second thing is what you do with the data you have. So things like multiple epochs. There was this period where everyone was super afraid of repeating data, like it was going to overfit immediately. And it turns out that for a decent amount of repetition, it's basically fine, especially if your data is good. So "we ran out of data" is a bit overstated. You can get more mileage out of what you've got than people think.

And then the third piece, which I find more interesting from a research standpoint, is the architectural and objective side. Like, are you actually extracting as much learning signal as you could be from each token? Things like different training objectives, UL2-style denoising, or thinking about how the model is spending its capacity. A lot of my earlier work was around this idea that the objective matters, not just the tokens. And I think that's still underexplored. We kind of collapsed onto next-token prediction because it's simple and it scales, and that's fine, but I don't think it's the end of the story.

The honest caveat I'd give is that data efficiency research is hard to do well because the signal is noisy at small scale. You run an ablation at 1B parameters and get a result, and then it doesn't transfer, or it transfers in a weird way. So you need a certain amount of compute just to even ask the question properly. Which is a little ironic for something that's supposed to be about efficiency.

But overall, yeah, I think it's going to matter more and more. If you're a smaller lab, it's basically the thing that lets you stay competitive, because you're never going to win on raw compute. You have to win on being smarter about what you feed the model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data quality, repetition, objectives, and compute, but does not frame data efficiency as identifying a concrete bug to fix.

astra-6.text:
I think data efficiency is a really important direction. A lot of progress comes from scaling the amount of data and compute, but there’s also the question of how much a model actually learns from each example. If you need to show it the same concept thousands of times, is that a limitation of the data, the training objective, or the model itself?

I’d look at those things together. Better data selection can help, but so can objectives that give the model a richer learning signal. And you have to measure whether it can generalize to something new, rather than just get better at examples similar to its training set. To me, that’s the interesting goal: learning more transferable structure from less experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data selection, learning objectives, and generalization, but does not frame data efficiency as identifying a concrete bug to fix.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much useful learning you get from each example, rather than just how many examples you have. You can improve that through better data selection, better training objectives, or architectures that make better use of the information available.

For example, if a model already handles a certain type of problem well, giving it more near-duplicates may not help much. The opportunity is to identify examples that teach it something it hasn’t learned, while preserving enough diversity that it generalizes.

And you have to measure that carefully. If better data efficiency requires a very expensive filtering pipeline, you may just be moving the cost somewhere else. I’d want to look at the whole process: the data, the compute, and ultimately how well the model performs on new problems.

r001.rationale: The response frames data efficiency as getting more useful learning from each example and improving data selection, objectives, and architectures. It does not describe identifying a concrete bug to fix.
